$comment: Settings for headless builds spawned by the watcher. Passed with --settings,
alongside --permission-mode bypassPermissions.
Two layers, because neither is sufficient alone:
permissions.deny  Explicit deny rules still apply under bypassPermissions,
so this catches the obvious cases even if the hook is
misconfigured. It cannot express 'anywhere except the
workspace' — deny beats allow and there is no negation —
so it names specific targets rather than trying to be
exhaustive. Note that Write(...) rules are inert: only
Edit(path) is matched by file permission checks, and Edit
rules cover all file-editing tools. A single leading / is
relative to this file's directory, so absolute paths use //.
Every Edit rule here must be narrow enough that it can
never contain a workspace. An earlier version denied
Edit(//C:/**) and Edit(~/**) as a stand-in for 'outside the
workspace'; that held only while the workspace lived on
another drive, and the day it moved under the home
directory those two rules silently denied every write to
the workspace itself and every build failed. Containment is
the hook's job — it knows the real root. This list names
system and credential directories only, and
scripts/build_settings.py refuses to generate a settings
file whose deny rules match a path inside the workspace.
hooks.PreToolUse  automation/hooks/guard.py, which does express it: every
Bash command is screened, every edit must land inside the
workspace, and credential paths are unreadable. Exit 2
blocks the call and hands the reason back to the model.
Neither reaches a subprocess. Once a permitted `python scripts/...` starts, it
can write anywhere this account can, and Claude Code's OS-level sandbox does
not run on native Windows. What actually bounds the blast radius: the pinned
working directory, the full NDJSON build log, automation/logs/builds/guard.log,
and the fact that a build only ever starts from an explicit Telegram reply.
